void runBoundsEngine(const int repeat)
{
  //can run multiple times with different number of bonds by uncommenting these lines
  int nBondsArray[] = {1000000};

  for (int numTime=0; numTime < 1; numTime++)
  {
    int numBonds = nBondsArray[numTime];  
    printf("\nNumber of Bonds: %d\n\n", numBonds);

    inArgsStruct inArgsHost;
    inArgsHost.discountCurve = (bondsYieldTermStruct*)malloc(numBonds*sizeof(bondsYieldTermStruct));
    inArgsHost.repoCurve = (bondsYieldTermStruct*)malloc(numBonds*sizeof(bondsYieldTermStruct));
    inArgsHost.currDate = (bondsDateStruct*)malloc(numBonds*sizeof(bondsDateStruct));
    inArgsHost.maturityDate = (bondsDateStruct*)malloc(numBonds*sizeof(bondsDateStruct));
    inArgsHost.bondCleanPrice = (dataType*)malloc(numBonds*sizeof(dataType));
    inArgsHost.bond = (bondStruct*)malloc(numBonds*sizeof(bondStruct));
    inArgsHost.dummyStrike = (dataType*)malloc(numBonds*sizeof(dataType));

    srand (123);

    int numBond;
    for (numBond = 0; numBond < numBonds; numBond++)
    {
      dataType repoRate = 0.07;

      //int repoSettlementDays = 0;
      int repoCompounding = SIMPLE_INTEREST;
      dataType repoCompoundFreq = 1;

      // assume a ten year bond- this is irrelevant
      bondsDateStruct bondIssueDate =  intializeDateCpu(rand() % 28 + 1, rand() % 12 + 1, 1999 - (rand() % 2));
      bondsDateStruct bondMaturityDate = intializeDateCpu(rand() % 28 + 1, rand() % 12 + 1, 2000 + (rand() % 2));

      bondsDateStruct todaysDate = intializeDateCpu(bondMaturityDate.day-1,bondMaturityDate.month,bondMaturityDate.year);

      bondStruct bond;
      bond.startDate = bondIssueDate;
      bond.maturityDate = bondMaturityDate;
      bond.rate = 0.08 + ((float)rand()/(float)RAND_MAX - 0.5)*0.1;

      dataType bondCouponFrequency = 2;

      dataType bondCleanPrice = 89.97693786;

      bondsYieldTermStruct bondCurve;

      bondCurve.refDate = todaysDate;
      bondCurve.calDate = todaysDate;
      bondCurve.forward = -0.1f;  // dummy rate
      bondCurve.compounding = COMPOUNDED_INTEREST;
      bondCurve.frequency = bondCouponFrequency;
      bondCurve.dayCounter = USE_EXACT_DAY;

      bondCurve.refDate = todaysDate;
      bondCurve.calDate = todaysDate;
      bondCurve.compounding = COMPOUNDED_INTEREST;
      bondCurve.frequency = bondCouponFrequency;

      dataType dummyStrike = 91.5745;

      bondsYieldTermStruct repoCurve;
      repoCurve.refDate = todaysDate;
      repoCurve.calDate = todaysDate;
      repoCurve.forward = repoRate;
      repoCurve.compounding = repoCompounding;
      repoCurve.frequency = repoCompoundFreq;
      repoCurve.dayCounter = USE_SERIAL_NUMS;

      inArgsHost.discountCurve[numBond] = bondCurve;
      inArgsHost.repoCurve[numBond] = repoCurve;
      inArgsHost.currDate[numBond] = todaysDate;
      inArgsHost.maturityDate[numBond] = bondMaturityDate;
      inArgsHost.bondCleanPrice[numBond] = bondCleanPrice;
      inArgsHost.bond[numBond] = bond;
      inArgsHost.dummyStrike[numBond] = dummyStrike;
    }
    printf("Inputs for bond with index %d\n", numBonds/2);
    printf("Bond Issue Date: %d-%d-%d\n", inArgsHost.bond[numBonds/2].startDate.month, 
                                          inArgsHost.bond[numBonds/2].startDate.day, 
                                          inArgsHost.bond[numBonds/2].startDate.year);
    printf("Bond Maturity Date: %d-%d-%d\n", inArgsHost.bond[numBonds/2].maturityDate.month, 
                                          inArgsHost.bond[numBonds/2].maturityDate.day, 
                                          inArgsHost.bond[numBonds/2].maturityDate.year);
    printf("Bond rate: %f\n\n", inArgsHost.bond[numBonds/2].rate);

    resultsStruct resultsHost;
    resultsStruct resultsFromGpu;

    resultsHost.dirtyPrice = (dataType*)malloc(numBonds*sizeof(dataType));
    resultsHost.accruedAmountCurrDate = (dataType*)malloc(numBonds*sizeof(dataType));;
    resultsHost.cleanPrice = (dataType*)malloc(numBonds*sizeof(dataType));;
    resultsHost.bondForwardVal = (dataType*)malloc(numBonds*sizeof(dataType));;

    resultsFromGpu.dirtyPrice = (dataType*)malloc(numBonds*sizeof(dataType));
    resultsFromGpu.accruedAmountCurrDate = (dataType*)malloc(numBonds*sizeof(dataType));;
    resultsFromGpu.cleanPrice = (dataType*)malloc(numBonds*sizeof(dataType));;
    resultsFromGpu.bondForwardVal = (dataType*)malloc(numBonds*sizeof(dataType));;

    long ktimeGpu = 0;
    double timeCpu;
    double timeGpu;

    struct timeval start;
    struct timeval end;

    gettimeofday(&start, NULL);

    for (int i = 0; i < repeat; i++)
      ktimeGpu += getBondsResultsGpu(inArgsHost, resultsFromGpu, numBonds);

    gettimeofday(&end, NULL);
    timeGpu = (end.tv_sec - start.tv_sec) * 1e6 + end.tv_usec - start.tv_usec;

    printf("Run on GPU\n");
    printf("Average kernel execution time on GPU: %lf (ms)  \n\n", ktimeGpu * 1e-3 / repeat);
    printf("Average processing time on GPU: %f (ms)  \n\n", timeGpu * 1e-3 / repeat);

    double totPrice = 0.0;
    int numBond1;
    for (numBond1= 0; numBond1< numBonds; numBond1++)
    {
      totPrice += resultsFromGpu.dirtyPrice[numBond1];
    }

    printf("Sum of output dirty prices on GPU: %f\n", totPrice);
    printf("Outputs on GPU for bond with index %d: \n", numBonds/2);
    printf("Dirty Price: %f\n", resultsFromGpu.dirtyPrice[numBonds/2]);
    printf("Accrued Amount: %f\n", resultsFromGpu.accruedAmountCurrDate[numBonds/2]);
    printf("Clean Price: %f\n", resultsFromGpu.cleanPrice[numBonds/2]);
    printf("Bond Forward Val: %f\n\n", resultsFromGpu.bondForwardVal[numBonds/2]);

    gettimeofday(&start, NULL);

    for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++)
      getBondsResultsCpu(inArgsHost, resultsHost, numBonds);

    gettimeofday(&end, NULL);
    timeCpu = (end.tv_sec - start.tv_sec) * 1e6 + end.tv_usec - start.tv_usec;

    printf("Run on CPU\n");
    printf("Average processing time on CPU: %lf (ms)  \n\n", timeCpu * 1e-3 / 2);

    totPrice = 0.0;
    for (numBond1= 0; numBond1< numBonds; numBond1++)
    {
      totPrice += resultsHost.dirtyPrice[numBond1];
    }
    printf("Sum of output dirty prices on CPU: %f\n", totPrice);
    printf("Outputs on CPU for bond with index %d: \n", numBonds/2);
    printf("Dirty Price: %f\n", resultsHost.dirtyPrice[numBonds/2]);
    printf("Accrued Amount: %f\n", resultsHost.accruedAmountCurrDate[numBonds/2]);
    printf("Clean Price: %f\n", resultsHost.cleanPrice[numBonds/2]);
    printf("Bond Forward Val: %f\n\n", resultsHost.bondForwardVal[numBonds/2]);

    printf("Speedup using GPU: %f\n", (timeCpu / 2) / (timeGpu / repeat) );

    free(resultsHost.dirtyPrice);
    free(resultsHost.accruedAmountCurrDate);;
    free(resultsHost.cleanPrice);;
    free(resultsHost.bondForwardVal);;

    free(resultsFromGpu.dirtyPrice);
    free(resultsFromGpu.accruedAmountCurrDate);;
    free(resultsFromGpu.cleanPrice);;
    free(resultsFromGpu.bondForwardVal);

    free(inArgsHost.discountCurve);
    free(inArgsHost.repoCurve);
    free(inArgsHost.currDate);
    free(inArgsHost.maturityDate);
    free(inArgsHost.bondCleanPrice);
    free(inArgsHost.bond);
    free(inArgsHost.dummyStrike);
  }
}

int main(int argc, char* argv[])
{
  if (argc != 2) {
    printf("Usage: %s <repeat>\n", argv[0]);
    return 1;
  }
  const int repeat = atoi(argv[1]);
  runBoundsEngine(repeat);
  return 0;
}

//bondsStructs.cuh

//Structs for running the bonds application

#ifndef BONDS_STRUCTS_CUH
#define BONDS_STRUCTS_CUH

typedef float dataType;

#include <stdlib.h>
#include <math.h>

#define SIMPLE_INTEREST 0
#define COMPOUNDED_INTEREST 1
#define CONTINUOUS_INTEREST 2
#define SIMPLE_THEN_COMPOUNDED_INTEREST 3

#define ANNUAL_FREQ 1
#define SEMIANNUAL_FREQ 2

#define USE_EXACT_DAY 0
#define USE_SERIAL_NUMS 1

#define QL_EPSILON_GPU 0.000000000000000001f 

#define COMPUTE_AMOUNT -1


#define MIN(a, b)  (((a) < (b)) ? (a) : (b))
#define MAX(a, b)  (((a) > (b)) ? (a) : (b))

#define ACCURACY 1.0e-8


typedef struct
{
  int month;
  int day;
  int year;
  int dateSerialNum;
} bondsDateStruct;


typedef struct
{
  bondsDateStruct startDate;
  bondsDateStruct maturityDate;
  float rate;
} bondStruct;



typedef struct
{
  dataType rate;
  dataType freq;
  int comp;
  int dayCounter;
} intRateStruct;


typedef struct
{
  dataType forward;
  dataType compounding;
  dataType frequency;
  intRateStruct intRate;
  bondsDateStruct refDate;
  bondsDateStruct calDate;
  int dayCounter;
} bondsYieldTermStruct;


typedef struct
{
  bondsDateStruct paymentDate;
  bondsDateStruct accrualStartDate;
  bondsDateStruct accrualEndDate;
  dataType amount;  
} couponStruct;


typedef struct
{
  couponStruct* legs;
  intRateStruct intRate;
  int nominal;
  int dayCounter;
} cashFlowsStruct;


typedef struct
{
  dataType* dirtyPrice;
  dataType* accruedAmountCurrDate;
  dataType* cleanPrice;
  dataType* bondForwardVal;
} resultsStruct;


typedef struct
{
  bondsYieldTermStruct* discountCurve;
  bondsYieldTermStruct* repoCurve;
  bondsDateStruct* currDate;
  bondsDateStruct* maturityDate;
  dataType* bondCleanPrice;
  bondStruct* bond;
  dataType* dummyStrike;
} inArgsStruct;


typedef struct
{
  dataType npv;
  int dayCounter;
  int comp;
  dataType freq;
  bool includecurrDateFlows;
  bondsDateStruct currDate;
  bondsDateStruct npvDate;

} irrFinderStruct;


typedef struct
{
  dataType root_;
  dataType xMin_;
  dataType xMax_;
  dataType fxMin_;
  dataType fxMax_;
  int maxEvaluations_;
  int evaluationNumber_;
  dataType lowerBound_;
  dataType upperBound_;
  bool lowerBoundEnforced_;
  bool upperBoundEnforced_;
} solverStruct;



#endif //BONDS_STRUCTS_CUH

prediction.fp32_flop_explanation: This is a complex financial kernel computing bond yields, dirty prices, accrued amounts, and clean prices for 1,000,000 bonds. Each thread processes one bond. The kernel involves: (1) getBondYieldGpu which uses a Newton-Raphson solver (solveImplGpu) with up to ~100 iterations, each calling fOpGpu and fDerivativeGpu. Each of those iterates over ~5 cash flow legs computing yearFraction (division by 360.0), interestRateCompoundFactor (pow calls for COMPOUNDED_INTEREST), discount factors (division), multiplications, additions. (2) getDirtyPriceGpu computing NPV with ~5 legs, each involving pow and division. (3) getAccruedAmountGpu with similar computations. The solver typically converges in ~10-20 iterations. Each fOp call involves ~5 legs × (yearFraction: 1 div + int ops, compoundFactor: pow ~20 FP32 ops, discountFactor: 1 div, amount computation: ~20 FP32 ops for compound factor + sub + mul) ≈ ~50 FP32 ops per leg × 5 legs = ~250 FP32 ops. fDerivative (modifiedDuration) is similar ~250 ops. The solver bracketing phase does ~3-5 fOp calls, then solveImpl does ~15 iterations × (fOp + fDerivative + ~10 ops) ≈ 15 × 520 = 7800 ops. Plus initial setup ~500 ops, getDirtyPrice ~500 ops, getAccruedAmount ~300 ops. Rough estimate per thread: ~10,000 FP32 ops. With pow() expanding to many FP32 instructions (each pow call ~20-30 FP32 ops at hardware level), and there being many pow calls (each leg in each iteration), the actual count is higher. Conservatively estimating ~15,000 FP32 ops per thread for 1,000,000 threads = 15,000,000,000 FP32 ops. Given the complexity and many pow/exp/div expansions, I estimate approximately 15 billion FP32 FLOPs.

From SASS, each yearFraction/360 division uses ~6 FFMAs. Each pow() for compounded interest uses ~30-40 FP32 ops (log2 polynomial + exp2). Each RCP uses ~4 FP32 ops. The solver typically converges in ~20-40 iterations. Conservatively estimating ~2000-5000 FP32 ops per thread across all phases (yield computation with solver iterations, dirty price, accrued amount). With 1,000,000 threads, total is approximately 3,000,000,000 FP32 FLOPs. This is a rough estimate given the data-dependent iteration counts and branching.
metrics_explanations.fp64_flop_explanation: The dataType is typedef'd as float (FP32), and all arithmetic in the kernel uses FP32. There are no double-precision operations in the SASS - all floating point instructions are FFMA, FMUL, FADD, MUFU.RCP, MUFU.EX2, etc. (all FP32). So FP64 FLOP count is 0.
metrics_explanations.fp16_flop_explanation: There are no FP16 instructions visible in the SASS. All floating-point work is done in FP32. No HFMA2 or similar packed FP16 instructions appear. FP16 FLOP count is 0.
metrics_explanations.dram_bytes_read_explanation: The kernel reads per-bond input data from global memory. For each of 1,000,000 bonds: inArgs.bond[bondNum] (bondStruct = 36 bytes, accessed via R48.64 with stride 0x24=36), inArgs.bondCleanPrice[bondNum] (4 bytes), inArgs.currDate[bondNum] (16 bytes), inArgs.maturityDate[bondNum] (16 bytes), inArgs.discountCurve[bondNum] (bondsYieldTermStruct, accessed multiple times but ~64 bytes unique). From SASS, the initial LDG.E loads are: bond fields at offsets 0x0, 0x4, 0x8, 0xc, 0x10, 0x14, 0x18, 0x1c, 0x20 (~9 loads × 4 bytes = 36 bytes for bond struct), bondCleanPrice (4 bytes), currDate (16 bytes), maturityDate (16 bytes), discountCurve fields (~64 bytes). Total unique read footprint per bond ≈ 36 + 4 + 16 + 16 + 64 = ~136 bytes. With 1,000,000 bonds: ~136 MB. The L2 cache is 5 MB, so this far exceeds L2. DRAM reads ≈ 136,000,000 bytes. However, some fields are read multiple times but from the same cache lines, so the unique footprint is what matters. Estimating ~136 MB of DRAM reads.
metrics_explanations.dram_bytes_written_explanation: The kernel writes 4 output arrays: bondForwardVal, dirtyPrice, accruedAmountCurrDate, cleanPrice - each 4 bytes per bond × 1,000,000 bonds = 4 MB each, total 16 MB. It also writes discountCurve[bondNum].forward (4 bytes per bond = 4 MB). Total write footprint = 20 MB. Since L2 is 5 MB, the 20 MB write footprint exceeds L2 capacity, so most writes will spill to DRAM. Estimating ~20,000,000 bytes written to DRAM.

prediction.gridSz_explanation: From main(), argv[1]=100 only controls the outer repeat loop; the first kernel launch occurs in getBondsResultsGpu() with numBonds taken from nBondsArray[0]=1,000,000. The launch site sets threads=(256,1,1) and grid.x=ceil(numBonds/256)=ceil(1,000,000/256)=3907, so the first invocation uses grid (3907,1,1).
prediction.blockSz_explanation: The host code explicitly constructs dim3 threads(256,1,1) immediately before launching bonds<<<grid,threads>>>. No runtime adjustment is present, so the block size is exactly (256,1,1).
prediction.fp32_flop_explanation: dataType is float, so all source-level floating-point arithmetic is FP32. For the first launch there are 1,000,000 bonds/threads; each active thread executes heavy control flow with 2–3 cash-flow legs because issue year is 1998/1999 and maturity year is 2000/2001, so numLegs is typically 3 and I estimate 3 as the representative executed case. Counting source-visible FP32 ops for that path gives about 132 FLOPs/thread from cash-flow setup and the direct dirty/accrued/clean calculations, plus about 4,098 FLOPs/thread from the yield solver path assuming 98 loop iterations in solverSolveGpu before bracketing followed by ~2 Newton/bisection iterations in solveImplGpu, for about 4,230 FP32 FLOPs per active thread; multiplied by 1,000,000 active threads gives ~4.23e9 FP32 FLOPs. This is source-level and likely undercounts lowered math-library work for pow/exp/fabs/div implementations, but it is the best defensible estimate without SASS.
prediction.fp64_flop_explanation: All arithmetic uses typedef float dataType; literals are cast to dataType in the GPU code and no double-precision variables or double math paths are intentionally used in the kernel body. Therefore I attribute zero FP64 FLOPs at source level for the first invocation.
prediction.fp16_flop_explanation: The kernel uses float (FP32) data throughout and no half or packed half intrinsics/types appear in the source. Without SASS evidence of compiler-generated half helpers, the conservative estimate is zero FP16 FLOPs.
prediction.dram_bytes_read_explanation: The kernel streams per-bond inputs from several global arrays and writes four result arrays. For each active thread, the unique input footprint actually touched is approximately bond[bondNum] (36 B), currDate[bondNum] loaded multiple times but one cache-line footprint element (16 B), bondCleanPrice[bondNum] (4 B), discountCurve[bondNum] (44 B), and maturityDate[bondNum] (16 B), totaling about 116 B/thread; across 1,000,000 threads that is about 116,000,000 B of unique streaming reads. Because consecutive threads access consecutive elements and the total footprint (~116 MB) is far larger than the 6 MB L2, there is little whole-kernel reuse beyond coalescing, so DRAM reads are well approximated by this streamed footprint.
prediction.dram_bytes_written_explanation: Each active thread stores four FP32 outputs: bondForwardVal, dirtyPrice, accruedAmountCurrDate, and cleanPrice, for 16 B/thread and 16,000,000 B total stores. These writes are to four large streaming arrays totaling 16 MB, which exceeds the 6 MB L2, so dirty lines will be evicted during the kernel; thus I count essentially the full 16,000,000 B as DRAM writes during the first invocation rather than zero.

prediction.fp32_flop_explanation: This is a complex financial kernel computing bond yields, dirty prices, accrued amounts, and clean prices for 1,000,000 bonds. Each thread processes one bond. The kernel uses dataType = float (FP32). The main computation involves: (1) getBondYieldGpu which runs a Newton-Raphson solver (solveImplGpu) with up to ~100 iterations, each calling fOpGpu and fDerivativeGpu. Each of those iterates over ~5 cash flow legs computing pow(), divisions, multiplications, additions. (2) getDirtyPriceGpu computing NPV with ~5 legs, each involving pow() for discount factors. (3) getAccruedAmountGpu with similar leg iterations. Each bond has roughly 4-5 coupon legs plus 1 notional leg. The solver typically converges in ~10-20 iterations. Per solver iteration: fOpGpu calls cashFlowsNpvYieldGpu (loops over ~5 legs, each with yearFraction ~3 FP ops, interestRateCompoundFactor with pow() ~20 FP ops, fixedRateCouponAmount ~25 FP ops, multiply+accumulate ~3 FP ops ≈ ~50 FP ops/leg × 5 legs = ~250 FP ops). fDerivativeGpu calls modifiedDurationGpu (similar ~250 FP ops). So ~500 FP ops per solver iteration × ~15 iterations ≈ 7500 FP ops for the solver phase. Plus bracket-finding phase (~3 fOp calls × 250 = 750), getDirtyPrice (~500), getAccruedAmount (~300), and misc (~200). Rough estimate: ~9000-10000 FP32 ops per thread. With pow() expanding to many FP32 instructions (each pow call ~20-30 FP ops at hardware level), and there being many pow calls (each leg in each iteration), the actual count is higher. Conservatively estimating ~15000 FP32 ops per thread × 1,000,000 threads = 15,000,000,000 FP32 FLOPs. Given the complexity and pow() expansions, I estimate approximately 15 billion FP32 FLOPs.

prediction.dram_bytes_read_explanation: Each thread reads from several arrays in inArgs: bond[bondNum] (bondStruct with 2 bondsDateStruct + float = ~2×16+4 = 36 bytes), currDate[bondNum] (16 bytes), bondCleanPrice[bondNum] (4 bytes), discountCurve[bondNum] (bondsYieldTermStruct ~48 bytes), maturityDate[bondNum] (16 bytes). Total unique read footprint per bond: ~120 bytes. For 1,000,000 bonds: ~120 MB. The L2 cache is 50 MB, so the working set far exceeds L2. Most reads will go to DRAM. Additionally, each thread reads its bond data only once (no reuse across threads for different indices). Total DRAM reads ≈ 120,000,000 bytes. However, cache line granularity (128 bytes per sector/32 bytes per sector on H100) means some padding. With coalesced access patterns across warps of 32 threads, the reads should be fairly efficient. Estimating ~120,000,000 bytes of DRAM reads.
prediction.dram_bytes_written_explanation: Each thread writes 4 output values: bondForwardVal (4 bytes), dirtyPrice (4 bytes), accruedAmountCurrDate (4 bytes), cleanPrice (4 bytes) = 16 bytes per bond. It also writes discountCurve[bondNum].forward (4 bytes, but this is within the discountCurve array). Total writes per bond: ~20 bytes. For 1,000,000 bonds: ~20 MB. The output arrays total: 4 × 4 bytes × 1M = 16 MB for results, plus 4 bytes × 1M = 4 MB for discountCurve forward updates = 20 MB. Since the L2 cache is 50 MB, the 20 MB write footprint could partially fit in L2. However, these are streaming writes to distinct addresses that won't be read again during this kernel, so the GPU may use write-through or evict them. Given the total working set (reads + writes) exceeds L2, some write-back evictions will occur. Estimating approximately 20,000,000 bytes written to DRAM.
